items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Support Multigrade Teaching?: Exploring Teachers’ Perceptions, Practices, and Challenges
items.abstract: Multigrade teachers face unique instructional challenges as they simultaneously manage learners from different grade levels, particularly in rural school settings where access to educational resources and technology is often limited. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been recognized as a potential tool for enhancing teaching and learning, limited research has explored how multigrade teachers in rural Philippine classrooms perceive, utilize, and navigate the integration of AI into their instructional practices. Addressing this gap, this study explored the perceptions, practices, perceived benefits, challenges, and support needs of multigrade teachers in integrating AI into their teaching. A qualitative case study approach was employed, involving ten (10) multigrade teachers from Kadingilan II District, Division of Bukidnon, during School Year 2026–2027. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and classroom observations. The findings revealed that teachers perceived AI as a supportive instructional assistant rather than a replacement for their professional roles. Based on their experiences, AI helped facilitate lesson preparation, differentiated instruction, and assessment. However, they emphasized that teacher judgment, creativity, and personal interaction with learners remain essential. The major challenges identified included limited internet connectivity, inaccuracies in AI-generated materials, cultural mismatches, and the risk of over-reliance on AI. To address these concerns, teachers practiced critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs, contextual adaptation of instructional materials, and peer collaboration. Furthermore, teachers identified practical, classroom-focused training, reliable internet connectivity, adequate technological devices, offline AI resources, and clear guidelines on ethical use, data privacy, and academic integrity as essential support mechanisms. The study concludes that AI has potential as a supplementary teaching tool in multigrade classrooms, particularly when supported by adequate resources, professional development, and responsible use. The reported benefits reflect teachers' experiences and perceptions rather than measured improvements in instructional effectiveness. These findings highlight the importance of context-responsive support in promoting meaningful and equitable AI integration in rural multigrade education.

items.title: Capability Is Not Authority: Decision Sovereignty and the Governance of Authority Delegated to AI Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems move from informing decisions to taking actions, the central governance question shifts from what a system can do to what it may do. This paper argues that capability and authority are distinct and that institutions lose control when they treat one as the other. Capability is the power to do something and is possessed by the actor. Authority is the legitimate right to decide and act; it is granted, bounded, accountable and revocable. A system cannot create legitimate authority for itself, but it can acquire de facto control over outcomes that no one granted. The paper develops the principle of Decision Sovereignty, under which an institution, not the systems it deploys, owns its decisions and their execution. It introduces measurement constructs from the Decision Sovereignty Governance Methodology (DSGM): an eight-level A-scale; Permitted AI Authority (PAA) and Effective AI Authority (EAA), read on the same scale; the Authority Gap between them; and Choice Architecture Control (CAC), which captures a system's power over the options humans see. It traces a sequence of failure, from authority drift through judgment displacement and an accountability vacuum to legitimacy collapse, and sets out a governing discipline of six authority questions that together form an Authority Charter. The paper positions Authority Exposure as a risk category that complements the AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF™) and closes with testable propositions. This working paper presents the core argument of the author's forthcoming book, Capability Is Not Authority: Why Institutions Must Remain Sovereign Over the Systems They Deploy (AIRIF Press), and builds on AIRIF™: AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF Press, 2026; ISBN 979-8-9982544-0-6) and the author's earlier working paper (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24323708).

items.title: CIVIL LIABILITY FOR INCORRECT LEGAL ADVICE PROVIDED THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: UZBEKISTAN'S LEGISLATION AND FOREIGN EXPERIENCE
items.abstract: This article examines civil liability for damages caused to individuals as a result of incorrect, outdated, or unreliable legal advice provided through artificial intelligence (AI). It explores the specific characteristics of damage arising from AI-based legal services, the identification of liable parties, the challenges of establishing damage and causation, and the legal status of service providers, developers, legal professionals, and users. The civil legislation of the Republic of Uzbekistan and regulatory frameworks governing artificial intelligence are comparatively analyzed in light of international experience. Based on the findings, the article proposes a differential liability model aimed at allocating liability according to the functional roles, obligations, fault, and causal contribution of each party to the occurrence of damage. The proposed model distinguishes between the mechanism for compensating the injured party and the internal recourse relationships among the parties involved.

items.title: CollaGraph: Mediating Human-AI Co-Creation of Interactive Mathematical Visualization through Structured Shared Context
items.abstract: Interactive visualizations (IVs) for mathematics are valuable for explanation and self-exploration, but their creation presents challenges, particularly for inexperienced creators. We present CollaGraph, a human-AI collaborative system for IV creation. Informed by formative studies that highlight the importance of complex dependencies and dynamic processes in IV creation, we propose the Dynamic Reliance Graph (DRG) as a node-based structured representation of IVs and incorporate it into CollaGraph. In CollaGraph, human creators and AI collaboratively iterate on shared structured content, including design plan lists and DRGs, through direct editing and comments. By compiling DRGs into IV previews, CollaGraph highlights the connections among components of the design plan, DRG, and IV outcome, thereby supporting the creative cycle of verification and modification. A user evaluation (N = 20) demonstrates that the DRG and other structured design elements facilitate IV creation, and that CollaGraph provides a supportive environment for IV co-creation while enhancing creativity and quality.

items.title: Competency‑based and emotional predictors of pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards the responsible use of Generative AI
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into initial teacher education requires an understanding not only of how frequently these tools are used, but also of the factors that shape their responsible adoption. This study examines how pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards responsible GenAI use is configured, identifying the competency-based resources and usage‑related variables that underpin it, as well as the role of anxiety across the dimensions assessed. A total of 298 pre‑service teachers from two Spanish universities participated, completing a validated 25‑item instrument comprising five dimensions: attitudes towards the use of AI for employability, digital flow in the responsible and safe use of AI, creativity to use AI responsibly, anxiety about using AI in future work contexts, and responsible use of AI for employability. Robust group comparisons, hierarchical regressions, and a network analysis with hierarchical clustering were conducted. The confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the instrument’s five‑factor structure. Creativity (β = 0.42) and digital flow (β = 0.37) emerged as the strongest predictors of responsible use, whereas usage frequency made no unique positive contribution. Anxiety was higher among women and younger participants; in the regression model it was associated with more favourable attitudes and higher digital flow, and with lower creativity only when these were controlled (a suppression effect). It occupied a peripheral position within the correlation network. The findings are synthesised in an exploratory two‑path empirical model that requires confirmatory testing. Initial teacher education may therefore benefit from fostering creative GenAI‑based experiences while deliberately addressing the emotional dimension of learning these technologies.
